meaning: A barrier is a physical part that provides a defined level of protection against contact with live parts from normal directions of access.
studyNote: Its protective purpose is to prevent access to live parts in normal use; the required degree of protection depends on the application.
distinction: An obstacle only prevents unintentional contact and does not prevent deliberate contact, so it is a weaker concept.

meaning: Basic insulation is insulation applied to live parts to provide basic protection in normal, fault-free conditions.
studyNote: Its safety role is protection against contact with live parts; insulation provided only so equipment functions correctly is not automatically basic insulation.
distinction: Basic insulation alone is not the same as double or reinforced insulation.

meaning: Basic protection is protection against electric shock when there is no fault in the installation or equipment.
studyNote: It deals with normal-condition access to live parts, using measures such as insulation, barriers or enclosures as applicable.
distinction: Fault protection deals with protection when a single fault has occurred.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide separates basic protection from fault protection when describing protection against electric shock.

meaning: A bonding conductor is a protective conductor whose purpose is equipotential bonding.
studyNote: Its role is to electrically connect conductive parts so their potentials are kept suitably close under the conditions addressed by the bonding measure.
distinction: The more specific current study term 'protective bonding conductor' identifies bonding provided for safety.

meaning: A circuit protective conductor (CPC) is the protective conductor that connects exposed-conductive-parts of equipment on a circuit back to the main earthing terminal.
studyNote: During an earth fault it is part of the fault-current return path used by the protective measure, helping protective devices disconnect the faulty circuit as required.
distinction: A CPC connects circuit equipment to the MET; an earthing conductor connects the MET to the earth electrode or other means of earthing; a bonding conductor connects parts for equipotential bonding.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide labels the CPC separately from earthing and bonding conductors in Figure 4.1 and later shows CPC continuity and ring-final-circuit test methods.

meaning: Class I equipment uses basic insulation and also provides a means to connect accessible exposed-conductive-parts to the installation protective conductor.
studyNote: The protective-conductor connection is part of the shock-protection strategy so a fault to exposed metal can be cleared by the protective system.
distinction: Class II equipment instead relies on additional insulation and normally has no protective-conductor connection to exposed metalwork.

meaning: Class II equipment provides shock protection by additional insulation precautions such as supplementary or equivalent insulation, without relying on a protective-conductor connection to exposed metalwork.
studyNote: The protection is built into the equipment construction rather than depending on the fixed wiring to earth exposed metalwork.
distinction: Class II is not the same as Class III: Class III relies on SELV supply.

meaning: Class III equipment relies on SELV for protection against electric shock and does not generate voltages above the SELV limits within the equipment.
studyNote: Its protective concept is therefore tied to the extra-low-voltage supply system, not simply to insulation class.

meaning: Double insulation means two independent insulation functions: basic insulation plus supplementary insulation.
studyNote: If the basic insulation fails, the supplementary insulation provides the additional protective layer.
distinction: Reinforced insulation provides an equivalent degree of protection as a single insulation system; double insulation is specifically basic plus supplementary insulation.

meaning: Earth is the conductive mass of the planet used as the conventional zero-potential reference.
studyNote: Earthing and earth-electrode concepts use this reference when connecting an installation or system to the general mass of Earth.

meaning: An earth electrode is a conductive part in electrical contact with Earth, either directly in soil or through a conductive medium such as concrete.
studyNote: It provides the physical interface between the electrical earthing arrangement and the general mass of Earth.
distinction: The earth electrode is not the same thing as the earthing conductor: the conductor connects the MET to the electrode or other means of earthing.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide explains the earth electrode's connection to the MET and gives current earth-electrode resistance measurement methods.

meaning: Earth electrode resistance is the electrical resistance between an earth electrode and the general mass of Earth.
studyNote: It is a key characteristic of electrode performance and forms part of the earth-fault path in arrangements that rely on an electrode, such as TT systems.
distinction: Do not confuse electrode resistance with total earth fault loop impedance, which includes the complete fault-current loop.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide describes loop-impedance and dedicated electrode-resistance test methods for earth electrodes.

meaning: Earthing, in this supplied definition, is the connection of exposed-conductive-parts of the installation to its main earthing terminal.
studyNote: It places accessible conductive equipment parts within the installation's protective earthing arrangement so fault protection can operate as designed.
distinction: The related term 'protective earthing' is the broader concept of earthing for safety; 'earthing conductor' names a particular conductor between the MET and the means of earthing.

meaning: The earthing conductor is the protective conductor between the main earthing terminal and the earth electrode or other means of earthing.
studyNote: It is the installation's connection from the MET to its external or supply-provided means of earthing.
distinction: It is not the CPC: the CPC runs from exposed-conductive-parts of circuit equipment to the MET.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide identifies the earthing conductor separately in the protective-earthing diagram, gives sizing guidance and includes it in continuity testing.

meaning: Electric shock is the dangerous physiological effect caused when electric current passes through a person or livestock.
studyNote: The definition describes the harmful effect; protective measures aim to prevent a dangerous current path through the body or limit its duration and magnitude.

meaning: Electrically independent earth electrodes are separated far enough that current through one does not significantly change the potential of the other electrode or electrodes.
studyNote: The definition is about electrical independence, not merely physical separation: the electrodes' potential zones must not significantly influence one another under the relevant current.

meaning: An enclosure is a part that protects equipment against specified external influences and, from any direction, provides basic protection against access to live parts.
studyNote: An enclosure therefore has both an equipment-protection role and a shock-protection role in the sense stated by the definition.
distinction: A barrier is defined mainly by preventing contact from usual directions of access; an enclosure surrounds equipment and also addresses external influences.

meaning: Equipotential bonding is the electrical connection of conductive parts so exposed-conductive-parts and extraneous-conductive-parts are maintained at substantially the same potential.
studyNote: The purpose is to reduce dangerous potential differences between parts that could be touched at the same time.
distinction: Protective equipotential bonding is equipotential bonding specifically provided for safety.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide's earthing-and-bonding section shows the relationship between exposed-conductive-parts, extraneous-conductive-parts, the MET and main or supplementary bonding conductors.

meaning: An exposed-conductive-part is a touchable conductive part of electrical equipment that is not normally live but can become live if a fault occurs.
studyNote: This is why exposed-conductive-parts are central to fault protection and are commonly connected to the protective-conductor system in Class I equipment.
distinction: An extraneous-conductive-part is not part of the electrical equipment or installation but can introduce a potential, usually Earth potential.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide labels exposed-conductive-parts in its protective-earthing diagram and discusses their relationship to bonding and simultaneous accessibility.

meaning: An extraneous-conductive-part is a conductive part that is not part of the electrical installation but is liable to introduce a potential, usually Earth potential, into the location.
studyNote: Typical assessment focuses on whether an incoming or structural conductive part can import Earth potential, because that may create a touch-voltage difference relative to exposed-conductive-parts.
distinction: A conductive item is not automatically extraneous merely because it is metal; it must be liable to introduce a potential and be outside the electrical installation.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide gives examples of metallic services and structural parts that may be extraneous-conductive-parts and explains when plastic services do not require main bonding.

meaning: Fault protection is protection against electric shock when a single fault has occurred.
studyNote: Its role is to keep touch voltages and their duration within the protective scheme's limits, commonly using protective earthing, protective equipotential bonding and automatic disconnection where that measure is used.
distinction: Basic protection covers fault-free conditions; fault protection covers the single-fault condition.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide describes fault protection as comprising protective earthing, protective equipotential bonding and automatic disconnection of supply where that method is used.

meaning: A functional earth is an earth connection provided so equipment or a system works correctly, rather than primarily for electrical safety.
studyNote: Examples of purposes can include signal reference, electromagnetic performance or equipment operation, but the defining point is that the connection serves function rather than shock protection.
distinction: Protective earthing is provided for safety; functional earthing is provided for function.

meaning: Insulation is suitable non-conductive material that encloses, surrounds or supports a conductor.
studyNote: In protection terminology, the particular role and construction of insulation determine whether it is basic, supplementary, double or reinforced.

meaning: An IT system has no direct connection between live parts and Earth, while the installation's exposed-conductive-parts are earthed.
studyNote: The first fault behaviour therefore differs from TN and TT systems, which have a source point directly connected to Earth.
distinction: IT, TN and TT describe the relationship of the source and exposed-conductive-parts to Earth; they are not names for individual protective devices.

meaning: The main earthing terminal (MET) is the central terminal or bar where the installation's protective conductors, protective bonding conductors and any functional-earthing conductors are connected to the means of earthing.
studyNote: It is the common reference point linking circuit protective conductors and bonding to the earthing conductor or supply earthing arrangement.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide repeatedly uses the MET as the connection point joining CPCs, bonding and the earthing conductor and notes its role in earthing arrangements and testing.

meaning: An obstacle is a part that prevents accidental or unintentional contact with live parts but does not prevent someone deliberately reaching the live part.
studyNote: It therefore provides only limited protection suited to circumstances where deliberate access is otherwise controlled.
distinction: A barrier provides a defined degree of protection against contact; an obstacle only prevents unintentional contact.

meaning: A protective bonding conductor is the protective conductor used to provide protective equipotential bonding.
studyNote: It connects the relevant conductive parts into the safety bonding arrangement so dangerous potential differences are reduced.
distinction: It is not the same as a CPC or earthing conductor, even though all are types of protective conductor.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide labels main and supplementary protective bonding conductors separately and includes their continuity in verification testing.

meaning: Protective conductor current is current flowing in a protective conductor, whether from normal leakage or from an insulation fault.
studyNote: The term describes current in the protective path; the cause matters because normal leakage and fault current have different implications.
distinction: Protective-conductor current is not limited to fault current.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide requires identification where circuits have high protective-conductor current and shows the corresponding warning notice.

meaning: Protective earthing is earthing provided specifically for electrical safety.
studyNote: It connects the required system, installation or equipment points to the earthing arrangement so the protective measures can control fault conditions.
distinction: Functional earthing serves operational purposes; protective earthing serves safety.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide devotes Section 4.1 to protective earthing and illustrates the protective-conductor network around the MET.

meaning: Protective equipotential bonding is equipotential bonding provided specifically for safety.
studyNote: It aims to limit hazardous potential differences between conductive parts that may be touched during a fault.
distinction: Equipotential bonding is the general concept; protective equipotential bonding is the safety application of it.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide explains main and supplementary protective bonding, including when incoming services are or are not treated as requiring bonding.

meaning: Protective multiple earthing (PME) is the UK TN-C-S supply arrangement in which the supply neutral is used as part of the connection between an installation's earthing conductor and Earth, with multiple earthing points on the network.
studyNote: For study, recognize PME as a particular supply-earthing arrangement associated with TN-C-S, not as a general synonym for every TN-C-S installation worldwide.
distinction: The quoted definition is tied to UK legislation and must not be treated as a Kenyan statutory requirement.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide discusses conductor sizing for TN-C-S (PME) supplies and gives typical TN-C-S earthing arrangements, while also telling installers to confirm the distributor's arrangement.

meaning: Reinforced insulation is a single insulation system that provides a degree of shock protection equivalent to double insulation under the relevant standard.
studyNote: It may contain multiple layers, but those layers are not treated as separately testable basic and supplementary insulation.
distinction: Double insulation is specifically basic plus supplementary insulation; reinforced insulation is one insulation system providing equivalent protection.

meaning: Shock current is current passing through a person or livestock with characteristics capable of producing dangerous physiological effects.
studyNote: It is the current through the body itself, whereas 'electric shock' describes the dangerous physiological effect produced.

meaning: Simultaneously accessible parts are conductive parts that a person—or livestock in a location intended for them—can touch at the same time.
studyNote: The concept matters because safety depends on limiting dangerous potential differences between parts that can be contacted simultaneously.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide discusses simultaneously accessible exposed-conductive-parts in relation to common earthing and touch-risk assessment.

meaning: Supplementary insulation is an independent layer of insulation added to basic insulation to provide fault protection.
studyNote: If basic insulation fails, this additional independent insulation provides the second protective layer used in double-insulation concepts.

meaning: A system describes the electrical source or sources together with the installation, and the TN, TT and IT labels classify how the source and exposed-conductive-parts relate to Earth.
studyNote: Use the letters to understand the earthing arrangement, fault-current path and protective-measure assumptions; the system label is not simply the name of a consumer unit or protective device.
distinction: TN, TT and IT are system-earthing classifications; TN-C, TN-S and TN-C-S further describe how neutral and protective functions are arranged.

meaning: In a TN system, a point of the source is directly earthed and the installation's exposed-conductive-parts are connected back to that earthed source point by protective conductors.
studyNote: The metallic protective return path is a defining feature of TN fault protection and influences fault-loop impedance and disconnection behaviour.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide shows typical TN arrangements and uses TN-C-S and TN-S assumptions in its standard final-circuit guidance.

meaning: In a TN-C system, neutral and protective functions are combined in one conductor throughout the system.
studyNote: The combined conductor is a PEN conductor, so the system does not maintain separate neutral and PE conductors throughout.

meaning: In a TN-C-S system, neutral and protective functions are combined in one conductor for part of the system and are separated for another part.
studyNote: A common supply example is PME, where the network uses a combined PEN conductor and the installation receives separate neutral and protective connections after the separation point.
distinction: TN-C-S describes conductor-function arrangement; PME is a particular UK earthing arrangement associated with TN-C-S.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide gives TN-C-S (PME) sizing and typical arrangement guidance and uses TN-C-S as a standard-circuit supply assumption.

meaning: In a TN-S system, neutral and protective conductors remain separate throughout the system.
studyNote: Fault current returns through the separate protective path rather than through a combined PEN conductor within the system.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide includes TN-S among the typical earthing arrangements and distinguishes it from TN-C-S.

meaning: Triplen harmonics are the odd multiples of the third harmonic—for example the 3rd, 9th, 15th and 21st components of the fundamental frequency.
studyNote: The term identifies a particular family of harmonic frequencies. When harmonic effects are being assessed, these components are treated as a distinct group rather than as the fundamental current.

meaning: In a TT system, the source has a directly earthed point, while the installation's exposed-conductive-parts are connected to a local earth electrode electrically independent of the source electrode.
studyNote: Because the installation's fault-current path includes Earth and the local electrode, electrode resistance and RCD-based fault protection are especially important practical concepts.
distinction: TT differs from TN because the installation does not rely on a metallic protective connection back to the source's earthed point.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide explains the role of the earth electrode in TT arrangements and includes TT assumptions in its final-circuit guidance.
